reason: Fusion proteins match the adjacent myoblast membranes and should help form the multinucleated muscle fibre described in the chapter.
expectation: The myoblasts will fuse into a long, multinucleated muscle cell.

effect: The myoblasts fused and matured into a multinucleated fibre with sliding filaments; its actin grip sites are still covered.
reaction: The distinction between one fibre and its many nuclei is useful.
reason: The calcium pulse spreads around the filaments, so it is the likely trigger for their pulling action.
expectation: Calcium will expose actin's grip sites and allow the fibre to pull.

effect: Calcium exposed the grip sites and initiated sliding; the filaments themselves did not shorten. The fibre still needs to become ready again.
reaction: The distinction between filament sliding and filament shortening is useful.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes should use ATP to return calcium to storage and end the pulse.
expectation: Calcium will be pumped back into storage, allowing the fibre to relax and become ready again.

effect: ATP-powered calcium pumping stopped pulling and left the fibre ready again; the next goal is to build and attach both muscles.
reaction: The need for ATP during relaxation is a useful distinction.
reason: The biceps sheaths have empty muscle-head spaces, so the relaxed fibre is a plausible component to fit into them.
expectation: The fibre will populate the biceps sheaths, forming a muscle connected to its tendons.

effect: The fibre needed connective matrix first; the resulting fascicles provide bundles for both muscles.
reaction: The distinction between a fibre's membrane and its surrounding connective layer is useful.
reason: The fascicles are muscle bundles that can fill the biceps sheaths and connect to their tendons.
expectation: The fascicles will form a biceps within the sheaths.

effect: The fascicles formed the two biceps heads, with connective tissue transmitting force to their tendons.
reaction: The force pathway makes the sheath and tendon connection clearer.
reason: The remaining fascicles should fill the three triceps head spaces, as they did for the biceps.
expectation: The fascicles will form a triceps with tendons ready for attachment.

effect: The remaining fascicles formed the three-headed triceps, leaving both muscles ready for attachment.
reaction: The different origins and joint crossings of the triceps heads are useful details.
reason: The biceps tendons need to attach to the movable arm skeleton across the elbow.
expectation: The biceps will attach to the skeleton at its shoulder and radius tendon routes.

effect: The biceps is attached across the front of the elbow; the arm assembly still needs an extensor.
reaction: The tendon pulling on the radius makes the flexion connection clear.
reason: The triceps is the remaining muscle and fits the arm assembly's extensor slot.
expectation: The triceps will attach across the elbow, completing the opposing muscle pair.

effect: The triceps filled the extensor slot, completing the arm and showing how tendon positions turn similar muscle pulls into opposite elbow movements.
reaction: The contrast between the two attachments makes the final construction satisfying.

mostWorthwhile.text: Triggering contraction and then relaxation made the sliding-filament mechanism and ATP's role in calcium pumping clear. The planned pictures distinguish filament overlap from filament shortening.

leastWorthwhile.text: Filling the two sets of sheaths was somewhat repetitive, although the different head and tendon arrangements added useful detail.

surprise.text: Relaxation required ATP-powered calcium pumping, and the fibre lengthened under an outside pull rather than actively pushing itself longer.

arbitrary.text: My attempt to put a fibre directly into the biceps sheaths missed the intermediate fascicle step. The compatibility feedback supplied the matrix combination, though the initial board did not make that requirement obvious.

continue.text: Yes. I would be interested to see how the assembled arm's structures work together, especially after the chapter connected microscopic pulling to movement at the elbow.
